model.name: Message
model.purpose: Provide the format-neutral context an agent needs to compose, address, send, carry, evidence, govern and interpret a discrete communication between agents across any channel.
model.scope_statement: A Message is a discrete, addressed communication act and its record: an originator releases identified content to one or more recipient endpoints over a channel, producing handling, delivery and disposition evidence. The model is an aggregate whose root is the message record and whose parts are content parts, addressing entries, handling-trace entries and evidence records. It is channel-neutral: electronic mail (RFC 5322/5321), instant messaging (RFC 6121), federated social activity (ActivityStreams 2.0), machine/event messaging (MQTT 5.0, CloudEvents), room-based messaging (Matrix) and clinical/business communication (FHIR Communication) are all projections of the same act. Storage and interface (JSON, YAML, Markdown, Git, MCP, MongoDB) are projections, not semantics.
in_scope: Message identity, classification, content parts, media typing and carriage of attachments or structured payloads
Originator and recipient roles, addressing visibility, recipient resolution, envelope-versus-content separation and handling trace
Conversation threading, reply and reference chains, derived/redistributed messages and request-response correlation
Transmission state, time points, delivery status records, registered delivery evidence and duplicate control
Origin authentication assertions, confidentiality/integrity protection scope and tamper evidence
Permission basis asserted at send time, opt-out signals, retention and disposition, redaction/deletion and access to retained copies
out_of_scope: The intrinsic content model, versioning and lifecycle of a carried document or dataset — the message owns only the carriage relation
The party/agent entity itself (person, organization, software agent) and its attributes
The durable contact-endpoint registry and address-scheme governance (owner, verification state, scheme syntax rules)
The standing consent/permission record about a subject and purpose, including its own grant/withdraw lifecycle
Channel-provider service entities, contracts, credentials, MTA/broker configuration and network operation
Cryptographic key material, trust anchors and certificate lifecycle management
Human language, terminology and translation semantics of message text

boundary_notes.distinction: MIME defines a body part and a Content-ID within the message entity, and FHIR Communication.payload is either inline content or a reference to a separately governed resource. The message therefore owns part structure, media typing, filename/disposition and payload digest, but not the referenced document's own identity, version history or retention rule.

RFC 5321 gives a mailbox meaning only inside SMTP; XMPP gives a JID meaning only inside XMPP; MQTT topics are broker-scoped. The message owns the addressing entry (role, submitted value, resolved value) as it existed for this message; the durable endpoint entity, its owner and its verification state belong to a sibling model.

ePrivacy Article 13 and GDPR Article 7 make consent a record about a subject, purpose and channel with its own demonstrability and withdrawal lifecycle, independent of any message. The message model records only the permission basis cited at send time and the opt-out signals the message itself carries (RFC 8058 List-Unsubscribe-Post).

CloudEvents describes an occurrence with source+id uniqueness and no inherent addressee; a message is directed to identified recipients and carries delivery obligation. An event becomes in-scope only when it is transported as an addressed message.

eIDAS Articles 43-44 attach legal presumptions only to a qualified electronic registered delivery service. The message model records the evidence object and its issuer, but conformity assessment and qualified status of the provider are governed elsewhere and must not be inferred from the presence of an evidence record.

NARA GRS 6.1 / Capstone assigns disposition by role and schedule item, which is an organizational instrument. The message model holds the applied disposition instruction reference and executed disposition events, not the schedule itself.

sources.title: RFC 5322: Internet Message Format
sources.relevance: Normative message identity (Message-ID MUST be unique), origination date, originator/destination/identification/informational/resent/trace field families.

sources.title: RFC 5321: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol
sources.relevance: Envelope (reverse-path/forward-path) versus content separation, Received trace obligations for relays, and null reverse-path for undeliverable-mail notifications.

sources.title: RFC 2045: MIME Part One — Format of Internet Message Bodies
sources.relevance: MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID and Content-Description; recursive multipart entity structure and part-level media typing.

sources.title: RFC 3464: An Extensible Message Format for Delivery Status Notifications
sources.relevance: Per-message (Original-Envelope-Id, Reporting-MTA, Arrival-Date) and per-recipient (Original-Recipient, Final-Recipient, Action, Status, Diagnostic-Code, Last-Attempt-Date) delivery evidence fields.

sources.title: RFC 8098: Message Disposition Notification
sources.relevance: Disposition types and modes, Original-Message-ID/Original-Recipient/Final-Recipient correlation, and the explicit warning that MDNs do not provide non-repudiation and can be forged or lost.

sources.title: RFC 8601: Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status

sources.title: RFC 6121: XMPP — Instant Messaging and Presence
sources.relevance: Non-email evidence for message typing (normal/chat/groupchat/headline/error), thread element with parent attribute, stanza id correlation and subscription-based contactability.

sources.title: RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers
sources.relevance: Message-carried opt-out: List-Unsubscribe-Post one-click semantics, HTTPS URI constraint, DKIM-signature coverage requirement and receiver consent obligation.

sources.title: Activity Vocabulary (ActivityStreams 2.0)
sources.relevance: Channel-neutral actor/object/target and to/bto/cc/bcc/audience addressing, the normative requirement that intermediaries MUST remove bto and bcc, inReplyTo, context, attachment and mediaType.

sources.title: Message Headers — Permanent Message Header Field Names registry
sources.relevance: Authoritative controlled vocabulary of message header field names with status (standard/informational/obsoleted), the correct governance point for extension metadata rather than local invention.

sources.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) Enhanced Status Codes Registry
sources.version_or_date: Registry, last updated 2024-12-06 (per RFC 5248, codes per RFC 3463)
sources.relevance: Class/subject/detail structure of delivery outcome codes: 2.x.x success, 4.x.x persistent transient failure, 5.x.x permanent failure — the basis for a channel-neutral outcome classifier.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS) — Articles 3(36)-(37), 43, 44
sources.relevance: Legal definition of electronic registered delivery service and the rebuttable presumptions of integrity, sending, receipt and accuracy of date and time attaching only to qualified services.

sources.title: Directive 2002/58/EC on privacy and electronic communications — Articles 5, 6, 9, 13
sources.version_or_date: Directive of 12 July 2002 (as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC)
sources.relevance: Prior-consent rule for direct-marketing electronic mail, the soft opt-in exception, the ban on concealing sender identity or omitting a valid opt-out address, confidentiality of communications and traffic-data erasure.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) — Articles 4(11), 5(1)(e), 7, 21, 30
sources.relevance: Consent definition and demonstrability, withdrawal parity, storage limitation, right to object to direct marketing and records of processing — governing constraints on message retention and permission evidence.

sources.title: FHIR R5 Communication resource
sources.version_or_date: FHIR v5.0.0 (Release 5), Standard for Trial Use
sources.relevance: Cross-domain confirmation of a channel-neutral message record: status/statusReason, category, priority, medium, topic/about, sent/received, sender/recipient, payload, inResponseTo, basedOn/partOf, and the executed-versus-requested boundary.

sources.title: MQTT Version 5.0
sources.relevance: Machine-messaging delivery guarantees (QoS 0/1/2 = at most once / at least once / exactly once), Message Expiry Interval, retained messages, Payload Format Indicator, Content Type, Correlation Data and Response Topic.

sources.title: Matrix Specification v1.16 — Client-Server API

sources.relevance: Public-authority evidence that message disposition can be assigned by originator role rather than per-item review, and that electronic messages are scheduled records under 44 U.S.C. ch. 29 and 36 CFR ch. XII.

sources.title: ETSI EN 319 522-2: Electronic Registered Delivery Services; Part 2: Semantic contents
sources.relevance: Named ERDS evidence set (SubmissionAcceptanceRejection, RelayAcceptanceRejection, NotificationForAcceptance, ConsignmentAcceptanceRejection, ContentConsignment, RetrievalNonRetrieval, DeliveryExpiration) and mandatory evidence components. NOTE: direct retrieval returned HTTP 403; content corroborated via ETSI abstracts and eIDAS Art. 43 — treated as a gap-flagged alignment, not verified conformance.

sources.relevance: Normative social object model: id IRI, attributedTo, to/bto/cc/bcc/audience, inReplyTo, published/updated, attachment, mediaType, natural-language maps, RFC 3339 timestamps, collections.

sources.relevance: Clinical or business record of information being transmitted, including planned and failed attempts. Status, medium, sent/received, payload, inResponseTo, sender, recipient. Distinct from AuditEvent and Encounter.

sources.relevance: Live retrieval of GDPR Article 7 text: demonstrable consent, distinguishable request, withdrawal as easy as grant, withdrawal does not undo prior lawful processing. Authentic instrument is CELEX:32016R0679. Secondary presenter is gdpr-info.eu.

bundles.name: Content and Payload
bundles.description: What the message says and carries: its identity, classification, part structure, media typing and carried payloads.
bundles.rationale: RFC 5322 separates the header section from the body, and MIME makes the body a recursive structure of typed entities; FHIR and CloudEvents confirm the same split between a communication record and its typed payload. Content is therefore a bundle distinct from addressing and from transit evidence.

layers.name: Message Core and Classification
layers.description: The identity of the message as a record and the classifiers that govern how it must be handled.

findings.name: Message identity and identifier provenance
findings.description: A message needs one durable identifier whose generator and uniqueness guarantee are known, plus any secondary identifiers assigned by transport or by the adopting Dimension. RFC 5322 requires the generator to guarantee msg-id uniqueness; CloudEvents requires source+id uniqueness; Matrix assigns a server-side event_id; SMTP separately carries an envelope identifier. These are different identifiers with different guarantors and must not be conflated.

questions.text: Which system generated the message's primary identifier and what is its uniqueness guarantee and scope?
Is identity single-valued or composite, and if composite which attributes form the key?
Which secondary identifiers exist for this message and who assigned each one?
answer_data: assigning role (originator, submission agent, relay, store)

questions.text: Does each recipient copy carry the same identifier, and how is a copy distinguished from the original record?

data_elements.name: messageIdentifier
data_elements.description: Primary identifier of the message as generated by the originating system, in the syntax of the governing channel standard.

data_elements.name: identifierScope
data_elements.description: Scope within which the identifier is guaranteed unique (global, source-scoped, room-scoped, submission-scoped).

data_elements.name: envelopeIdentifier
data_elements.description: Transport-assigned submission identifier used to correlate status reports with a submission transaction, distinct from the content identifier.

data_elements.name: alternateIdentifiers
data_elements.description: Additional identifiers assigned by stores, relays or the adopting Dimension, each with its assigner.

artifacts.name: Message record
artifacts.description: The aggregate root: the persisted representation of one communication act, binding identity, classification, content parts, addressing entries and evidence references.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Authoritative master-system message identifier from the originating channel (msg-id, event_id, broker-assigned id); otherwise a governed composite of source and id; otherwise a UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension, never a timestamp.

findings.name: Subject, classification, priority and sensitivity
findings.description: Classifiers that drive handling: topic/subject, functional category, urgency and sensitivity. FHIR distinguishes category, priority, topic and about; XMPP types a stanza as chat, groupchat, headline, normal or error; ActivityStreams types the activity itself. These are separate axes and collapsing them loses handling semantics.

questions.text: Which classification axes apply to this message and which are mandatory for the channel?
What urgency or priority is asserted, by whom, and does it change handling or retention?
What sensitivity or confidentiality label applies and what handling constraint does it impose?
How is the human-readable subject distinguished from the machine-resolvable topic or about-reference?

data_elements.name: subjectText
data_elements.description: Human-readable subject or summary of the message.

data_elements.name: messageCategory
data_elements.description: Functional category of the communication (alert, notification, reminder, chat, headline, instruction).

data_elements.name: priority
data_elements.description: Asserted urgency of the message from a governed code list.

data_elements.name: sensitivityLabel
data_elements.description: Confidentiality or sensitivity classification constraining handling and redistribution.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Classifiers are attributes of the message record rather than separately custodied objects; they have no independent identity, no separate custodian and are never transmitted or retained apart from the message. The governed code lists they draw on belong to a classification/registry sibling model.

findings.name: Channel type and provider
findings.description: A channel is the transport medium used or intended, not the message. RFC 5321 defines SMTP client, server, relay, gateway, originating and delivery systems. ActivityPub uses inbox and outbox OrderedCollections and optional sharedInbox. FHIR Communication.medium records how the communication was conveyed. Gatewaying may transform headers and envelopes in ways forbidden to a pure relay. Channel type is classification here; credentials and live sockets are out of scope.

questions.text: Which channel type and provider actually carried this message, and was the hop an origin, relay, gateway or delivery system?
answer_data: channel-type, provider-ref, hop-role enum origin | relay | gateway | delivery, protocol-profile.

questions.text: If federated social transport, which outbox accepted the activity and which inbox or sharedInbox was posted?
If a clinical communication, what medium codes describe how information was shared?
answer_data: List of FHIR medium CodeableConcepts with system and code.

data_elements.name: channel-type
data_elements.description: smtp | submission | activitypub-inbox | fhir-medium | imap-store | xmpp | matrix | sms | postal | broadcast | other.

data_elements.name: provider-ref
data_elements.description: Organization or service that operates the channel.

data_elements.name: protocol-profile
data_elements.description: EHLO extensions, ActivityPub c2s vs s2s, FHIR medium coding.

data_elements.name: gatewayed-from-channel
data_elements.description: Prior channel if this copy was gatewayed.

data_elements.name: shared-inbox-iri
data_elements.description: ActivityPub sharedInbox used for public or followers delivery.

artifacts.name: channel-descriptor
artifacts.description: Channel type, provider, protocol profile and whether this hop is origin, relay, gateway or delivery.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Per the model identifier priority: authoritative origin identifier (Message-ID, ActivityPub object id IRI or FHIR identifier), else a governed global IRI, else a Dimension-assigned UUID or ULID; a date is never an identifier.

layers.name: Content Structure and Payload
layers.description: The recursive part structure of message content, its media typing, and the payloads it carries by value or by reference.

findings.name: Body parts, media typing and alternative representations
findings.description: MIME makes a message body a recursive tree of entities, each with its own Content-Type, transfer encoding, Content-ID and optional description; MQTT types payload with a Payload Format Indicator and Content Type; Matrix types content by msgtype. Interpretation requires knowing the part tree, the declared type of each node and which sibling parts are alternatives rather than additions.

questions.text: What is the ordered part tree of this message and what is the structural role of each node?
answer_data: structural role (alternative, mixed, related, signed, encrypted)

questions.text: What media type, subtype, parameters and transfer encoding are declared for each part, and were they verified against the octets?
Which part is the canonical representation when several alternatives express the same content?
What natural language and character encoding apply to each textual part?

data_elements.name: partPath
data_elements.description: Position of the part within the recursive content tree.

data_elements.name: partMediaType
data_elements.description: Declared media type, subtype and parameters of the part.

data_elements.name: contentTransferEncoding
data_elements.description: Encoding transformation applied to the part body; defaults to 7bit when absent.

data_elements.name: partContentIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the MIME entity, used for intra-message references such as related parts.

data_elements.name: partByteSize
data_elements.description: Size of the decoded part body in octets.

artifacts.name: Message content part
artifacts.description: One typed entity in the message content tree, holding either a leaf body or a nested multipart structure.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Content-ID where the channel assigns one; otherwise the message identifier combined with the ordered part path, which is stable only within the message aggregate.

findings.name: Carried payloads: attachments and structured data
findings.description: A message carries payloads either by value or by reference. MIME Content-Disposition supplies filename and attachment role; FHIR payload is content as attachment, reference or coded concept; CloudEvents adds datacontenttype and dataschema for machine-interpretable payloads. The message owns the carriage relation and payload digest, not the referenced object's own lifecycle.

questions.text: Is each payload carried by value or by reference, and if by reference what resolves the reference and for how long?
For structured payloads, which schema governs the data and how is schema identity conveyed?
What digest or checksum binds the payload to this message, and over what canonical octets was it computed?
Who owns the carried object and does carriage transfer any rights or obligations?

data_elements.name: carriageMode
data_elements.description: Whether the payload is embedded by value or referenced externally.

data_elements.name: payloadReference
data_elements.description: Resolvable reference to the carried object when carriage is by reference.

data_elements.name: presentedFilename
data_elements.description: Filename presented for the payload by the disposition mechanism, which is advisory and untrusted.

data_elements.name: payloadSchemaIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the schema the structured payload conforms to.

data_elements.name: payloadDigest
data_elements.description: Cryptographic digest of the payload octets with the algorithm used.

artifacts.name: Payload carriage entry
artifacts.description: The record binding one carried payload to the message: carriage mode, reference, presented name, declared type, schema and digest.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Payload Content-ID or referenced resource identifier where present; otherwise the message identifier plus part path. The carried object's own authoritative identifier is owned by the document/record sibling model.

bundles.name: Parties and Addressing
bundles.description: Who released the message, on whose authority, to which endpoints, with what visibility, and by which handling path.
bundles.rationale: RFC 5321 makes the envelope legally and operationally distinct from the header section; RFC 5322 separates From, Sender and Reply-To; ActivityStreams normatively requires intermediaries to strip bto and bcc; RFC 3464 separates Original-Recipient from Final-Recipient. Addressing therefore carries independent semantics and cannot be folded into content.

layers.name: Originator and Sending Authority
layers.description: The roles on the sending side and the authority under which the message was released.

findings.name: Originator roles, delegation and reply routing
findings.description: RFC 5322 distinguishes the author (From), the actual releasing agent (Sender, required when From lists several addresses) and the intended reply target (Reply-To); SMTP separately carries the return path used for failure reports. ActivityStreams distinguishes actor from attributedTo, and FHIR distinguishes sender from subject. Delegated and machine-generated sending is the normal case for agents, so authority must be explicit.

questions.text: Who authored the message and who actually released it, and are they the same party?
If the message was sent on behalf of another party, what authorises that and is the authorisation still valid at send time?
Where should replies and where should failure reports be directed, and why do they differ?
Is the originator identity fully disclosed as required for the message purpose and jurisdiction?

data_elements.name: authorParty
data_elements.description: Party asserted as the author of the message content.

data_elements.name: releasingAgent
data_elements.description: Party or software agent that actually transmitted the message, required when the author is plural or differs from the releaser.

data_elements.name: replyTarget
data_elements.description: Address to which replies should be directed if different from the author address.

data_elements.name: returnPath
data_elements.description: Envelope originator to which non-delivery reports are sent; a null value marks the message itself as a report.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Originator roles are reference attributes on the message record pointing at parties governed by the agent/party sibling model; the delegation instrument that authorises sending is itself an artifact of an authority/mandate sibling model, not of the message. Nothing here is separately custodied as a message-owned object.

layers.name: Recipient Addressing
layers.description: The recipient entries on a message, their visibility rules, and how submitted addresses resolve to actual delivery targets.

findings.name: Recipient roles and addressing visibility
findings.description: Primary, secondary and blind recipient roles carry different disclosure obligations. ActivityStreams states that intermediaries MUST remove bto and bcc before redistribution; RFC 5322 treats Bcc handling as sender-agent dependent. A recipient copy therefore legitimately differs from the originator copy, and the model must record which variant it holds.

questions.text: What addressing role does each recipient entry carry and is that role visible to other recipients?
Which addressing variant does this stored copy represent — originator view, recipient view or redistributed view?
Which addressing fields must be removed or masked before this message is forwarded, archived or exported?
When the target is a topic, room or audience rather than a named party, how is the addressed set determined and bounded?

data_elements.name: recipientReference
data_elements.description: Party or endpoint addressed by this entry.

data_elements.name: recipientRole
data_elements.description: Addressing role of the entry: primary, secondary, blind primary, blind secondary or audience.

data_elements.name: copyVariant
data_elements.description: Which addressing view this stored copy represents, since blind entries are removed on redistribution.

data_elements.name: targetScope
data_elements.description: Non-party target such as a topic filter, room or channel to which the message was addressed.

artifacts.name: Recipient addressing entry
artifacts.description: One recipient slot on a message, holding role, submitted value, resolved value and visibility flags; the unit against which per-recipient delivery evidence is recorded.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Message identifier plus recipient ordinal, or the transport's per-recipient correlation value (Original-Recipient) where one exists; the durable endpoint entity is identified by the contact-endpoint sibling model.

findings.name: Recipient resolution, expansion and redirection
findings.description: The address a sender submitted is often not the address that received the message. RFC 3464 keeps Original-Recipient for sender correlation and Final-Recipient as seen by the reporting agent, and defines expanded and relayed actions for list expansion and gatewaying. Losing the submitted value breaks correlation, consent scoping and suppression.

questions.text: What address did the sender submit for this recipient and what address actually received the message?
Did this recipient entry expand into multiple targets, and is the resulting set knowable to the sender?
Was the message redirected or forwarded after acceptance, and does downstream evidence still correlate to the original entry?
Does a permission or suppression decision taken on the submitted address still hold for the resolved address?

data_elements.name: submittedRecipientAddress
data_elements.description: Recipient address exactly as supplied by the sender, retained for correlation and permission scoping.

data_elements.name: resolvedRecipientAddress
data_elements.description: Address at which the handling agent accepted or attempted delivery.

data_elements.name: expansionIndicator
data_elements.description: Whether the entry expanded to multiple downstream targets.

data_elements.name: addressTypeCode
data_elements.description: Address type qualifier (for example rfc822, x400, jid, topic) needed to interpret the address value.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Resolution outcomes are qualifying attributes of the recipient addressing entry artifact and of delivery status records; they are never custodied or transmitted independently. Creating a separate artifact would duplicate the delivery status notification, which already carries these fields normatively.

layers.name: Envelope and Handling Path
layers.description: The separation between routing instructions and message content, and the recorded path the message actually travelled.

findings.name: Envelope versus content separation
findings.description: RFC 5321 states the delivery reverse-path is simply the address given in MAIL FROM, independent of any header field, and that content is what is sent in DATA. Header From and envelope originator routinely differ, which is the basis of both legitimate forwarding and impersonation. Any model that stores only one of the two loses the ability to reason about authenticity and bounce routing.

questions.text: What are the envelope originator and envelope recipients, and how do they differ from the header-declared parties?
Which of the two identifier sets was authenticated, and by which mechanism?
Is envelope data retained after delivery, and under what rule may it be erased?
For non-mail channels, which construct plays the envelope role and what is its retention behaviour?

data_elements.name: envelopeOriginator
data_elements.description: Transport-level originator used for routing and failure reporting; may be null on report messages.

data_elements.name: envelopeRecipients
data_elements.description: Transport-level recipient set actually used for routing, which may differ from declared destination fields.

data_elements.name: envelopeEquivalentConstruct
data_elements.description: Channel-specific construct fulfilling the envelope role (SMTP paths, XMPP to/from, MQTT topic, Matrix room).

findings.inline_only_rationale: Envelope values are transient routing state that standards deliberately do not persist in the message content; where they are preserved they appear inside the handling trace record or the delivery status notification, both of which are modelled as artifacts. Minting a separate envelope artifact would assert a persistence that RFC 5321 does not require and that ePrivacy traffic-data rules actively discourage.

findings.name: Handling trace and custody path
findings.description: Each relay must prepend its own trace entry and must not alter existing ones, producing an append-only, reverse-chronological custody path; Matrix achieves the equivalent through a signed event graph with prev_events. The trace is the primary provenance evidence for when and where a message was handled, and is the main source of traffic data subject to erasure duties.

questions.text: What is the ordered sequence of handling agents and what did each one assert about time and origin?
What guarantees that trace entries were not altered or reordered after the fact?
Which trace entries were created inside the trust boundary of the recording organisation and which are untrusted assertions?
When must trace and traffic data be erased or anonymised, and what is the lawful basis for retaining it longer?

data_elements.name: handlingAgentIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the agent that handled the message at this hop.

data_elements.name: handlingTimestamp
data_elements.description: Time asserted by the handling agent for this hop, recorded with explicit offset.

data_elements.name: tracePosition
data_elements.description: Position of the entry in the handling sequence; trace entries are prepended, so order is significant.

data_elements.name: withinTrustBoundary
data_elements.description: Whether the entry was created inside the recording organisation's administrative management domain.

artifacts.name: Handling trace record
artifacts.description: Append-only sequence of custody entries describing each agent that received, relayed or gatewayed the message, with asserted times and trust classification.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Message identifier plus trace position; where the channel signs each hop, the hop signature or event identifier is authoritative. Trace entries are never identified by timestamp alone because clocks across hops are unsynchronised and assertions may be forged.

bundles.name: Conversation Structure
bundles.description: How messages relate to one another: threads, reply chains, derived messages and request-response correlation.
bundles.rationale: RFC 5322 defines In-Reply-To and References; XMPP defines a thread element with a parent attribute; Matrix defines m.relates_to reply and thread relations; FHIR defines inResponseTo, basedOn and partOf. Conversation structure is expressed by independent, sometimes conflicting mechanisms and needs its own bundle.

layers.name: Threading and Continuity
layers.description: Grouping messages into conversations and reconstructing reply order from per-message pointers.

findings.name: Thread identity, membership and participation scope
findings.description: Threads are constructed differently per channel: XMPP carries an opaque thread identifier with an optional parent, Matrix uses a room plus a thread relation to a root event, and mail has no thread field at all and must be reconstructed from References. Thread identity is therefore either channel-assigned or derived, and the model must record which.

questions.text: Is the thread identifier channel-assigned or derived by reconstruction, and by which algorithm?
What determines whether a message belongs to the thread, and can membership change after the fact?
Who participates in the thread, and does a participant see the whole thread or only the messages addressed to them?
How are thread splits, merges and subthreads represented without breaking existing references?

data_elements.name: threadIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the conversation grouping to which the message belongs.

data_elements.name: threadAssignmentMode
data_elements.description: Whether thread membership was asserted by the channel or derived by reconstruction.

data_elements.name: parentThreadIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of a parent conversation when the thread branches from an earlier one.

data_elements.name: threadRootMessage
data_elements.description: Message that roots the thread, where the channel defines threads by reference to a root.

artifacts.name: Conversation thread
artifacts.description: The grouping object for messages exchanged in one conversation, holding thread identity, root, participation window and split/merge history.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Channel-assigned thread or room identifier where one exists; otherwise a UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension together with the reconstruction algorithm reference, so that derived threads are never mistaken for asserted ones.

findings.name: Reply and reference chains
findings.description: Mail carries In-Reply-To for the immediate parent and References for the ancestor chain; ActivityStreams carries inReplyTo; Matrix carries an explicit reply relation. These pointers can be missing, wrong, or point at messages the holder cannot resolve, so chain reconstruction must be treated as fallible evidence rather than fact.

questions.text: Which message does this one reply to, and is that parent resolvable in the current holding?
What ancestor chain is asserted, and does it agree with the parent pointer and the thread assignment?
How is a broken, forged or circular reference chain detected and represented?
Does the reply quote or transclude the parent content, and does that create a second copy under separate custody?

data_elements.name: inReplyToMessage
data_elements.description: Identifier of the immediate message being replied to.

data_elements.name: referenceChain
data_elements.description: Ordered ancestor identifiers asserted by the sender for conversation reconstruction.

data_elements.name: referenceResolutionStatus
data_elements.description: Whether each asserted reference resolves within the current holding.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Reply pointers are attributes of the message record itself and are transmitted only as part of it; the reconstructed conversation graph is a derived projection over those attributes, materialised through the conversation thread artifact rather than as an independent object.

layers.name: Derived Messages and Correlation
layers.description: Messages produced from other messages, and the correlation of a response to its request.

findings.name: Forwarded, resent and corrected messages
findings.description: RFC 5322 resent fields explicitly reintroduce a message to new recipients without making it a new message, and require their own resent identifier and date; Matrix supports replacement and redaction relations. Redistribution changes the accountable sender and the addressing view while preserving the original content, so the derivation relation must be typed.

questions.text: What kind of derivation produced this message: forward, resend, correction, replacement or recall?
Who is accountable for the redistributed message, and does original authorship survive the derivation?
Was the original content preserved unaltered, and how is any alteration recorded?
Does the channel support withdrawal of an already-released message, and what does withdrawal actually guarantee?

data_elements.name: derivationType
data_elements.description: Typed relation to a predecessor message: forward, resend, correction, replacement or withdrawal.

data_elements.name: sourceMessage
data_elements.description: Identifier of the message from which this one derives.

data_elements.name: redistributionIdentifier
data_elements.description: Distinct identifier assigned to the act of redistribution, separate from the original message identifier.

data_elements.name: redistributionTime
data_elements.description: Time the redistribution act occurred, with explicit offset.

findings.inline_only_rationale: A derived message is itself an instance of the message record artifact; what is new here is only the typed relation and the redistribution identifier carried on that record. Introducing a separate derivation artifact would create a second identity for the same communication act.

findings.name: Request-response correlation and expected reply
findings.description: Machine messaging makes the reply contract explicit: MQTT carries Correlation Data and a Response Topic, XMPP correlates by stanza id, and FHIR distinguishes basedOn (the order being fulfilled) from inResponseTo. For agent-to-agent communication this is the difference between a conversational reply and a contractual response to a request.

questions.text: What correlation token binds this response to its request, and who minted it?
Where should the response be sent, and is that target different from the request's reply address?
Is a response required, optional or forbidden, and what happens if none arrives within the expected window?
Does this message fulfil a prior request or order, and is that fulfilment complete or partial?

data_elements.name: correlationToken
data_elements.description: Opaque value binding a response to the request that elicited it.

data_elements.name: responseTarget
data_elements.description: Address, topic or endpoint at which the response is expected.

data_elements.name: responseObligation
data_elements.description: Whether a response is required, optional or not expected.

data_elements.name: fulfilsRequest
data_elements.description: Reference to the request, order or plan this message fulfils, distinct from a conversational reply pointer.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Correlation values live only on the request and response message records and have no independent custody, transmission or retention. The request itself is a message record; representing the correlation as its own artifact would duplicate that record without adding a governable object.

bundles.name: Transit and Evidence
bundles.description: The state of the message in transit, its time points, and the evidence produced about delivery and recipient disposition.
bundles.rationale: RFC 3464 and RFC 8098 define two structurally different evidence records with different issuers and different reliability; eIDAS attaches legal presumptions only to registered delivery evidence; MQTT defines delivery guarantees at the protocol level. Evidence is therefore a bundle in its own right and must not be reduced to a status field.

layers.name: Transmission State and Time
layers.description: The lifecycle state of a message and the distinct time points that mark its progress.

findings.name: Message state model and terminal outcomes
findings.description: FHIR types Communication.status from an event status value set including in-progress, completed, not-done, entered-in-error and unknown; DSN types the transport action as failed, delayed, delivered, relayed or expanded. These are different state machines — one about the communication act, one about a delivery attempt for one recipient — and both are needed.

questions.text: At which level is state asserted — the whole message, one recipient entry, or one delivery attempt?
Which states are terminal, which are retryable, and what distinguishes a permanent from a transient failure?
Which state transitions are permitted and which agent role may assert each transition?
How is a message recorded as entered in error or never actually sent, without deleting the record?

data_elements.name: messageStatus
data_elements.description: Lifecycle state of the communication act as a whole.

data_elements.name: recipientDeliveryAction
data_elements.description: Outcome of the delivery attempt for one recipient: failed, delayed, delivered, relayed or expanded.

data_elements.name: statusReason
data_elements.description: Coded or textual reason accompanying a non-routine state.

data_elements.name: failureClass
data_elements.description: Whether a failure is permanent, persistent transient or a success confirmation, from the enhanced status class.

findings.inline_only_rationale: State values are attributes carried on the message record and on delivery status notification artifacts; the notifications themselves are the custodied objects. Modelling state as an artifact would either duplicate the delivery status notification or invent a record that no cited standard transmits.

findings.name: Distinct time points and clock trust
findings.description: Standards deliberately keep several times apart: the origination date is when the creator finished the message for transmission, not when transport occurred; DSN adds Arrival-Date, Last-Attempt-Date and Will-Retry-Until; FHIR separates sent from received; Matrix records origin_server_ts. RFC 3339 requires an explicit offset and reserves -00:00 for unknown local offset.

questions.text: Which distinct time points are recorded for this message and what does each one actually mean?
Is event time separated from observation or ingestion time, and which one is authoritative for ordering?
Whose clock produced each timestamp and what is known about its trustworthiness or synchronisation?
Is the sender's local offset known, and how is an unknown offset represented rather than guessed?
Does the message expire, and what happens to it and to its evidence at expiry?

data_elements.name: originationTime
data_elements.description: Time the creator completed the message for transmission, with explicit offset per RFC 3339.

data_elements.name: submissionTime
data_elements.description: Time the message was released into the channel by the sending agent.

data_elements.name: receiptTime
data_elements.description: Time a handling agent or recipient endpoint accepted the message.

data_elements.name: observationTime
data_elements.description: Time the recording system observed or ingested the fact, kept separate from the event time it describes.

data_elements.name: expiryInterval
data_elements.description: Interval or instant after which the message must not be delivered and may be discarded.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Time points are qualifying attributes of the message record, the handling trace record and the evidence artifacts already defined; no cited standard transmits or custodies them as a standalone object, and doing so would fragment the very correlation these fields exist to support.

layers.name: Delivery Evidence
layers.description: Records produced by transport and delivery services about what happened to the message, and the guarantees they do and do not confer.

findings.name: Delivery status records and outcome coding
findings.description: A DSN is a distinct message reporting per-message fields (reporting agent, arrival date, envelope identifier) and per-recipient fields (final recipient, action, status code, diagnostic code, retry window). The enhanced status code is a three-part class/subject/detail structure maintained in an IANA registry, which is the correct vocabulary source rather than local status strings.

questions.text: Which agent issued the status record and was it authorised to speak for the delivery attempt?
What outcome code was reported, from which registry, and how does it map to the model's outcome classifier?
How does the status record correlate back to the original message and to a specific recipient entry?
Can multiple, later or contradictory status records exist for the same recipient, and which one prevails?

data_elements.name: reportingAgent
data_elements.description: Agent that attempted delivery and issued the status record.

data_elements.name: enhancedStatusCode
data_elements.description: Three-part class/subject/detail outcome code from the governed registry.

data_elements.name: diagnosticDetail
data_elements.description: Channel-specific diagnostic text accompanying the outcome code.

data_elements.name: retryWindowEnd
data_elements.description: Time until which further delivery attempts will be made for a delayed outcome.

artifacts.name: Delivery status record
artifacts.description: A machine-readable report about the outcome of a delivery attempt for one or more recipients, issued by a handling agent and correlatable to the original submission.
artifacts.identity_strategy: The report's own message identifier where it is transmitted as a message; otherwise the original envelope identifier plus final recipient plus reporting agent. Reports are ordered by issue time but never identified by it.

findings.name: Registered delivery evidence and legal presumption
findings.description: An electronic registered delivery service transmits data and provides evidence about its handling, including proof of sending and receiving. Under eIDAS the presumptions of integrity, sending, receipt and accuracy of date and time attach only to qualified services; ETSI EN 319 522 names the evidence set (submission, relay, notification, consignment acceptance or rejection, retrieval, expiration). Evidence must not be conflated with ordinary status reports.

questions.text: Which named evidence event does this record attest, and at which point of the transfer?
Who issued the evidence, under which issuing policy, and is that issuer a qualified provider?
What legal presumption, if any, does this evidence carry and in which jurisdiction?
How is the evidence cryptographically bound to the exact payload it attests?
How long must the evidence remain verifiable, and what preserves its validity beyond signature expiry?

data_elements.name: evidenceEventType
data_elements.description: Named evidence event attested, from the registered delivery evidence set.

data_elements.name: evidenceIssuer
data_elements.description: Delivery service provider that issued the evidence.

data_elements.name: qualifiedStatusAsserted
data_elements.description: Whether the issuer is asserted to be a qualified provider, and the listing that supports the assertion.

data_elements.name: evidenceEventTime
data_elements.description: Time of the attested event as sealed by the issuer, with explicit offset.

artifacts.name: Registered delivery evidence token
artifacts.description: A signed or sealed record issued by a registered delivery service attesting a named event in the transfer, bound to the payload digest and the identified sender and recipient.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Evidence identifier assigned by the issuing service, which is the authoritative master system for this object; the subject message identifier and payload digest provide correlation but never identity.

findings.name: Delivery guarantee level and duplicate control
findings.description: MQTT makes the guarantee explicit and bounded: at most once may lose messages, at least once may duplicate, exactly once is assured by a four-step handshake. CloudEvents pushes deduplication onto consumers via source+id uniqueness. An agent must know the guarantee before treating an absent acknowledgement as non-delivery or a repeat as a new message.

questions.text: What delivery guarantee did the channel provide for this message, and who selected it?
How is a duplicate delivery detected and what is the idempotency key?
What may be concluded from the absence of an acknowledgement under this guarantee level?
Does the channel retain the message for later subscribers or offline recipients, and for how long?

data_elements.name: deliveryGuaranteeLevel
data_elements.description: Asserted guarantee: at most once, at least once or exactly once.

data_elements.name: idempotencyKey
data_elements.description: Key used to recognise redelivery of the same message rather than a new one.

data_elements.name: deliveryAttemptCount
data_elements.description: Number of delivery attempts recorded for a recipient entry.

data_elements.name: channelRetentionBehaviour
data_elements.description: Whether the channel holds the message for later or offline delivery, and for how long.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Guarantee level and idempotency key are protocol-level qualifiers recorded on the message record and on delivery status records; the acknowledgement packets that implement them are transient protocol units that no cited standard requires to be preserved as separate governed objects.

layers.name: Recipient Disposition
layers.description: What the recipient did with the message, and the strict limits on what such reports prove.

findings.name: Disposition notifications and read evidence
findings.description: MDN reports a disposition (displayed, deleted, dispatched, processed) together with an action mode (manual or automatic) and a sending mode; Matrix reports read receipts and read markers. RFC 8098 states plainly that MDNs do not provide non-repudiation with proof of delivery, can be forged as easily as ordinary mail, may be lost, and may be bypassed by the recipient, and it requires recipient consent before sending.

questions.text: What disposition is reported, and does it mean the content was actually presented to a person?
Did the sender request a disposition notification, and did the recipient consent to sending one?
What is the evidential weight of this report and which specific claims may not be made from it?
What does a disposition report disclose about the recipient, and is that disclosure permissible?
How is the notification target validated to prevent amplification or mail-bombing abuse?

data_elements.name: dispositionType
data_elements.description: Reported handling of the message by the recipient: displayed, deleted, dispatched or processed.

data_elements.name: dispositionMode
data_elements.description: Whether the action and the notification were manual or automatic.

data_elements.name: originalMessageIdentifier
data_elements.description: Identifier of the message the disposition report refers to.

data_elements.name: evidentialWeight
data_elements.description: Recorded classification of how far the report may be relied on, given known forgeability.

artifacts.name: Disposition notification record
artifacts.description: A recipient-side report of what was done with a message, carrying disposition type, mode, correlation identifiers and an explicit reliability qualification.
artifacts.identity_strategy: The report's own message or event identifier assigned by the reporting system; correlation uses the original message identifier and original recipient, which are not identity because a single message may yield several conflicting reports.

bundles.name: Trust and Protection
bundles.description: Whether the message really came from whom it claims, and whether its content was kept confidential and unaltered.
bundles.rationale: RFC 8601 defines a normative way to record authentication outcomes and a strict trust-boundary rule; MIME, Matrix and eIDAS all bind integrity to specific octets under specific canonicalisation. Authenticity and confidentiality are independent of delivery outcome and require a separate bundle.

layers.name: Origin Authentication
layers.description: Recorded outcomes of mechanisms that test whether the asserted origin is genuine.

findings.name: Origin authentication results and trust boundaries
findings.description: Authentication-Results records, per method, which identifier was tested and with what result, stamped by an authentication service identifier. The specification requires handling agents to delete any instance claiming to originate inside their trust boundary when it arrives from outside, and warns that consumers should not interpret the field unless configured to trust the stamper.

questions.text: Which authentication methods were evaluated, against which identifier, with what result?
Which authentication service stamped the result and is it inside the consuming organisation's trust boundary?
How are forged or externally injected authentication assertions detected and removed?
What downstream decision may be based on the result, and what must not be inferred from a pass?
answer_data: fallback when result is none or temperror

data_elements.name: authenticationServiceIdentifier
data_elements.description: Token identifying the service that performed the authentication checks.

data_elements.name: authenticationMethod
data_elements.description: Mechanism evaluated, such as domain signature, path authorisation, alignment policy or reverse lookup.

data_elements.name: authenticationResult
data_elements.description: Outcome value from the governed result vocabulary.

data_elements.name: authenticatedIdentifier
data_elements.description: The specific identifier that the method actually authenticated, which may not be the visible author address.

artifacts.name: Authentication results assertion
artifacts.description: A stamped record of authentication outcomes for one message, attributable to a named authentication service and scoped to a trust boundary.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Message identifier plus authentication service identifier plus evaluation time, because a message legitimately carries several assertions from different services; the assertion has no independent master identifier.

layers.name: Confidentiality and Integrity
layers.description: What protection was applied to which parts of the message, and what integrity can be demonstrated afterwards.

findings.name: Protection scope, integrity and post-hoc verifiability
findings.description: Protection is scoped: MIME allows signing or encrypting individual entities, Matrix encrypts room events end to end while leaving structural fields visible, and eIDAS requires protection of transmitted data against unauthorised alteration. What is protected, what remains observable, and whether verification is still possible after storage transformations are separate questions.

questions.text: Which parts of the message are confidentiality-protected and which metadata remains observable to intermediaries?
Can integrity still be verified from the stored form, and what canonicalisation is required to do so?
Which storage or transport transformations would invalidate the integrity evidence, and are they prohibited?
If content is end-to-end protected, what remains discoverable, auditable or retainable by the custodian?
answer_data: governance consequence for retention and disclosure

data_elements.name: protectionMechanism
data_elements.description: Mechanism applied to protect confidentiality or integrity of message content.

data_elements.name: protectionScope
data_elements.description: Which parts or fields the protection covers, and which remain in clear.

data_elements.name: canonicalisationRule
data_elements.description: Rule under which the protected octets were canonicalised, required for later verification.

data_elements.name: lastVerificationOutcome
data_elements.description: Outcome and time of the most recent integrity verification of the stored form.

artifacts.name: Protected content object
artifacts.description: The signed or encrypted representation of message content together with the parameters needed to verify or decrypt it later, excluding key material itself.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Message identifier plus protected part path; where the protection mechanism assigns its own object or signature identifier, that identifier is authoritative. Keys and trust anchors are identified by a key-management sibling model.

bundles.name: Custody and Governance
bundles.description: The permission under which contact was made, the opt-out signals the message carries, and how retained copies are kept, disposed of and disclosed.
bundles.rationale: ePrivacy Article 13 conditions unsolicited electronic contact on prior consent and a valid opt-out address; GDPR imposes storage limitation, demonstrable consent and a right to object; NARA schedules electronic messages as records; RFC 8058 makes opt-out a message-carried mechanism. Governance is therefore intrinsic to the message, not an afterthought.

layers.name: Permission and Suppression
layers.description: The basis relied on to contact a recipient and the opt-out mechanics carried by the message.

findings.name: Permission basis asserted at send time
findings.description: Direct-marketing electronic mail generally requires prior consent, with a narrow soft opt-in for existing customers of similar products who were given an easy objection route; GDPR requires the controller to be able to demonstrate consent and makes withdrawal as easy as giving. The message model records the basis cited and the evidence pointer at send time; the consent record itself is governed by a sibling model.

questions.text: On what basis was this recipient contacted for this purpose on this channel?
answer_data: basis code (consent, soft opt-in, contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest)

questions.text: When was the permission state evaluated relative to release, and was a fresher state available?
Does the basis cover this purpose and this resolved address, or only the address originally submitted?
What would be produced to demonstrate the permission if challenged, and where is it held?

data_elements.name: permissionBasisCode
data_elements.description: Legal or policy basis relied on to contact the recipient for the message's purpose.

data_elements.name: permissionEvidenceReference
data_elements.description: Pointer to the externally governed consent or permission record relied on.

data_elements.name: communicationPurpose
data_elements.description: Declared purpose of the message, against which permission scope is assessed.

data_elements.name: permissionEvaluationTime
data_elements.description: Time at which the permission state was checked, with explicit offset.

findings.inline_only_rationale: The consent record is deliberately kept outside this model: GDPR Article 7 gives it its own demonstrability and withdrawal lifecycle bound to a subject and purpose, not to any message. What the message owns is the basis code, purpose and evidence pointer captured at release, which are attributes of the message record and of the send event.

findings.name: Message-carried opt-out and suppression signals
findings.description: Opt-out is partly a property of the message itself: a valid address for cessation requests must be present, and one-click unsubscribe requires an HTTPS URI, a specific post header and DKIM coverage of both headers, with receivers obtaining user consent before posting. Suppression outcomes then feed back into future send decisions.

questions.text: Does the message carry a valid, working cessation mechanism appropriate to its purpose and channel?
Are the opt-out headers covered by the message's authentication signature so a receiver may act on them?
When an opt-out is exercised, what scope does it suppress and within what deadline must it take effect?
answer_data: suppression scope (endpoint, subject, purpose, all channels)

questions.text: How does a suppression signal interact with a still-valid permission record or a non-marketing message?

data_elements.name: optOutMechanism
data_elements.description: Type of cessation mechanism carried by the message.

data_elements.name: optOutTarget
data_elements.description: Address or URI at which a cessation request is accepted.

data_elements.name: optOutSignatureCoverage
data_elements.description: Whether the opt-out fields are covered by a valid origin signature.

data_elements.name: suppressionScope
data_elements.description: Extent of suppression resulting from an exercised opt-out.

artifacts.name: Suppression entry
artifacts.description: A record that a given endpoint, subject or purpose must not be contacted, created from an exercised opt-out or objection and consulted before any subsequent send.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Suppressed endpoint or subject reference plus scope plus effective-from instant; where a master consent system exists, that system's suppression identifier is authoritative and this entry is a cached projection.

layers.name: Retention and Disposal
layers.description: How long message records are kept, on what basis, and how they are redacted or destroyed.

findings.name: Retention basis, appraisal and disposition
findings.description: Personal data must not be kept in identifiable form longer than necessary, while public-sector electronic messages are scheduled records that may be appraised by originator role rather than item-by-item. Traffic data carries its own erasure duty distinct from content. Retention is therefore multi-basis and can be assigned at different granularities.

questions.text: What retention rule applies to this message, at what granularity, and who assigned it?
Do content, addressing metadata, traffic data and evidence share one retention period or different ones?
What event starts the retention clock and what event ends it?
What suspends disposition, who may impose and lift that suspension, and how is it evidenced?

data_elements.name: retentionRuleReference
data_elements.description: Reference to the schedule item or policy rule governing this message's retention.

data_elements.name: retentionPeriod
data_elements.description: Duration for which the component must be kept, per component where periods differ.

data_elements.name: dispositionDueDate
data_elements.description: Computed date at which disposition becomes due.

data_elements.name: dispositionHold
data_elements.description: Active suspension of disposition with its imposing authority and scope.

artifacts.name: Applied disposition instruction
artifacts.description: The record binding a message or a class of messages to a retention rule, the computed disposition date, any holds, and the executed disposition outcome.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Schedule item identifier from the authoritative records-management system plus the message or class identifier it is applied to; a UUID assigned by the adopting Dimension is used only where no records system identifier exists.

findings.name: Redaction, deletion and what survives
findings.description: Deletion is rarely total: Matrix redaction removes content fields while preserving event identity, sender, timestamp and room, precisely so the conversation graph stays intact. Copies held by recipients and intermediaries are outside the sender's control, so the model must state which copies an erasure action actually reaches.

questions.text: Which fields are removed by a redaction and which are deliberately preserved, and why?
Which copies does a deletion or redaction actually reach, and which remain beyond the actor's control?
What tombstone or audit evidence remains after destruction, and is it sufficient to prove lawful disposal?
How does redaction interact with signatures, digests and delivery evidence over the redacted content?

data_elements.name: erasureActionType
data_elements.description: Type of erasure performed: redaction, content deletion, full destruction or anonymisation.

data_elements.name: preservedFields
data_elements.description: Fields deliberately retained after redaction to keep referential structure intact.

data_elements.name: erasureTime
data_elements.description: Time the erasure action was executed, with explicit offset.

data_elements.name: erasureAuthority
data_elements.description: Role or instrument authorising the erasure.

artifacts.name: Redaction or destruction record
artifacts.description: Evidence that an erasure action occurred, naming the target message, the fields removed, the surviving tombstone, the authority and the execution time.
artifacts.identity_strategy: The redaction event's own identifier where the channel assigns one; otherwise target message identifier plus execution time plus executing role, since a message may be redacted more than once by different custodians.

layers.name: Access and Disclosure
layers.description: Who holds a copy of a message, who may read it, and how disclosure is authorised and audited.

findings.name: Copy custody, access control and disclosure
findings.description: Every message exists as several copies with different custodians and different visible content, because blind addressing is stripped on redistribution and confidentiality of communications restricts interception and access by anyone other than the users concerned. Access decisions therefore attach to a specific copy, not to an abstract message.

questions.text: Which custodians hold a copy of this message and how does each copy differ from the originator's?
Who may read each copy by default, and which role grants exceptions?
Under what authority may a message be disclosed to a third party, and what is recorded about the disclosure?
What access and disclosure events must be audited, and how long is the audit trail itself kept?
When the message contains personal data about a third party, how are their rights handled without breaching the correspondents' confidentiality?

data_elements.name: copyCustodian
data_elements.description: Party or system holding this copy of the message and accountable for it.

data_elements.name: defaultAccessRule
data_elements.description: Baseline rule determining who may read this copy absent an explicit grant.

data_elements.name: accessGrant
data_elements.description: Explicit, time-bounded grant of access to a party beyond the default rule.

data_elements.name: disclosureEvent
data_elements.description: Record of a disclosure to a third party, with authority, scope and time.

artifacts.name: Message copy holding
artifacts.description: A custodied instance of a message in one holding system, with its variant, access rule, grants, disclosure history and audit trail.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Holding-system item identifier from the authoritative store where one exists; otherwise message identifier plus custodian reference. The message identifier alone is insufficient because it is shared across all copies.

functions.name: Compose message
functions.description: Assemble a message record: mint or accept an identifier, set classification, build the typed content part tree and bind carried payloads by value or reference.
inputs: content parts with declared media types
preconditions: Identifier generator and its uniqueness scope are known
Each part has a declared media type
Delegation is authorised where the releaser differs from the author
effects: A message record exists with a resolvable identifier and a validated part structure
Origination time is recorded with an explicit offset

functions.name: Resolve and classify recipients
functions.description: Turn submitted recipient values into addressing entries with roles and visibility flags, retaining the submitted value alongside any resolved value.
preconditions: Address type qualifier is known for each value
Blind-addressing handling rule for the target channel is known
effects: Submitted and resolved addresses are both retained for correlation
Entries requiring removal on redistribution are flagged

functions.name: Check contact permission and suppression
functions.description: Evaluate whether each recipient may be contacted for the declared purpose on the chosen channel, consulting the external permission record and the suppression entries.
preconditions: Purpose is declared
Suppression source is reachable and its freshness is known
effects: Recipients without a valid basis are removed before release
The cited basis and evaluation time are recorded on the message

functions.name: Submit message to a channel
functions.description: Release the message into a channel, forming the envelope, selecting the delivery guarantee and recording the submission time and envelope identifier.
preconditions: Permission check has passed for every remaining recipient
A valid cessation mechanism is present where the purpose requires one
Return path for failure reports is set
effects: The message becomes irrevocable except where the channel supports withdrawal
Envelope values are recorded separately from content

functions.name: Record a handling event
functions.description: Append a custody entry describing an agent that received, relayed or gatewayed the message, without altering existing entries.
preconditions: The trace store is append-only
Trust boundary of the recording organisation is defined
effects: Provenance of the message's path is extended
Entries originating outside the trust boundary are marked untrusted

functions.name: Record a delivery status report
functions.description: Ingest a transport status report, map its outcome code to the model's classifier and correlate it to the originating submission and recipient entry.
preconditions: Correlation identifiers are present or recoverable
Outcome code registry is available
effects: Per-recipient delivery outcome is updated
Contradictory or superseded reports are ordered by the supersession rule

functions.name: Register registered-delivery evidence
functions.description: Store a sealed evidence token from a registered delivery service, bind it to the payload digest and record the issuer, issuing policy and asserted qualified status.
preconditions: Evidence seal or signature can be validated
Issuer identity resolves to a listed provider or is recorded as unverified
effects: The evidence is preserved with its verification state
No legal presumption is asserted unless qualified status is evidenced

functions.name: Record recipient disposition
functions.description: Ingest a disposition notification or read receipt, correlate it to the message and recipient, and attach an explicit evidential-weight qualification.
preconditions: Notification target was validated against the return path
Recipient consent to report was obtained where required
effects: Disposition is recorded without any non-repudiation claim
Absence of a report is not converted into a negative delivery fact

functions.name: Evaluate and stamp origin authentication
functions.description: Run configured authentication methods, stamp the results with the authentication service identifier and remove untrusted assertions claiming to originate inside the trust boundary.
preconditions: Authentication service identifier is configured
Trust boundary is explicitly defined
effects: Downstream consumers can attribute results to a named service
Injected assertions from outside the boundary are deleted and audited

functions.name: Assemble conversation view
functions.description: Group messages into a thread using channel-asserted identifiers where available and reconstruction from reference chains otherwise, marking derived membership as such.
preconditions: Reconstruction algorithm is declared and versioned
Access rules of the requesting party are known
effects: A conversation is presented with asserted and derived membership distinguished
Messages the requester may not read are excluded rather than silently merged

functions.name: Apply retention and compute disposition
functions.description: Bind the message and its components to retention rules, compute disposition dates per component and honour any active hold.
preconditions: The governing schedule or policy rule is resolvable
Clock-start event has occurred
effects: Content, traffic data and evidence receive their own retention treatment
Disposition is suspended while a hold is active

functions.name: Redact or destroy a message copy
functions.description: Execute an authorised erasure on a specific copy, removing designated fields while preserving the structural tombstone, and record what evidence the action invalidates.
preconditions: No active hold applies to the target
Authority for erasure is evidenced
Reachable and unreachable copies have been identified
effects: Designated content is irrecoverable in the treated copy while references remain resolvable
Integrity evidence covering removed content is marked invalidated rather than silently broken

functions.name: Disclose a message copy
functions.description: Release a message copy to an authorised requester under a stated authority, applying required masking and writing an audit entry.
preconditions: Disclosure authority is valid and in scope
Blind-addressing and third-party data have been assessed for masking
effects: Access outside the default rule is recorded with authority, scope and time
Confidentiality obligations toward non-requesting correspondents are preserved

functions.name: Deliver, relay or gateway
functions.description: Accept envelope responsibility, add trace, relay unmodified or gateway with allowed transformations, expand aliases or lists according to their distinct DSN rules, and POST federated activities to inboxes.
inputs: Alias, mailing-list or collection expansion targets
outputs: Federated activity POSTed to target inboxes or sharedInbox
preconditions: Responsibility is accepted only after a success response at end of mail data
effects: Responsibility to deliver or report failure is accepted
Trace is added; relays do not otherwise modify message data while gateways may transform
Aliases and lists are expanded under their distinct DSN rules

functions.name: Update, delete, undo or recall
functions.description: Apply Update, Delete/Tombstone, Undo or a channel-specific recall; record entered-in-error or stopped for clinical communications; do not claim universal unsend.
outputs: Update, Delete/Tombstone, Undo or channel-specific recall record
preconditions: The channel supports the mutation and the actor owns the object
effects: Origin-side object updated, tombstoned or withdrawn
No claim of universal unsend; federated or delivered copies may remain

functions.description: Create a new message with In-Reply-To/References or inReplyTo/inResponseTo, inherit or amend addressing, and trigger inbox forwarding when the origin cannot expand owned collections.
